name: Benin
summary_text: Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults are legal in Benin. Article 545 of the new Penal Code, in force since 2018, provides an equal age of consent regardless of sex, while retaining higher penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex.  Benin law provides no prohibition of discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and no protection against discrimination based on gender identity in particular. Legal gender recognition is impossible, so a trans visitor has no recognition pathway to rely on and no statutory protection to invoke.  Benin does not recognise LGBTQI+ couples and families. The sole exception sourced is the grant of diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats. Article 104(d) of the Children’s Code, Law 2015-08, bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption.  The United States State Department 2023 human rights report found hostility toward LGBTQI+ persons, most pronounced outside major urban areas, with routine refusal of medical care, including hormone treatment, and of social services. Other sources report regular refusal of LGBTQ-related care such as gender-affirming hormone therapy and regular denial of general care such as malaria treatment.  Physical danger comes principally from private actors. Reports describe anti-gay lynchings as commonplace, alongside arbitrary detention, physical and sexual violence and degrading treatment. Violence is described as mostly committed by civilians rather than state authorities, while police rarely pursue perpetrators.  Victims conceal sexual orientation or gender identity when reporting violence or discrimination for fear of mistreatment by police. Lesbian, bisexual and queer women are reported to rarely report to police, indicating no reliable protection machinery for a visitor who needs help.  A narrow set of electronic and data rules exists. Article 552 of Law No. 2017-20 on the Digital Code, in place since 2018, punishes provocation of discrimination, hatred or violence based on sexual orientation through an electronic communications network or computer system with one year of imprisonment and a fine of five million CFA francs, or one of those penalties only. Article 394 of the same law and Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law prohibit processing personal data revealing sex life or sexual orientation, the latter without express consent. Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 of 2012 requires business leaders to prevent, end and punish sexual or sexist acts or behaviour based on sex or real or perceived sexuality that infringe the rights and dignity of women or girls.  Enforcement history qualifies the legal status. Benin’s representative stated in the 2008 review that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered under the provisions then on the books. The general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct. Benin rejected recommendations to improve the situation of LGBTQ persons in the 2012 review. In the 2023 Universal Periodic Review the government accepted two of fifteen recommendations concerning LGBTQ persons, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against persons living with HIV.  Religious institutions contribute to hostility. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries. Priests are documented as calling transgender people demons. Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques take part in homophobic preaching. Imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion practices, often coerced by families.  LGBTI organisations cannot register in Benin. Public events have nevertheless occurred, including a public International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event organised by LGBTQ associations in Cotonou at the Institut Français on 17 May 2013, attended by 200 people.  Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restriction for LGBT people.  Since about 2020 the Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre has operated temporary accommodation reported as 20 places, through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region passed by 2024. The scale of that caseload relative to capacity underlines the level of social violence, while the facility itself is youth shelter infrastructure rather than a visitor service.

sources.title: U.S. Department of State 2023 Human Rights Report on Benin
sources.documents: Enforcement/living conditions; found LGBTQI+ community especially outside major urban areas faced hostility, and discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons was common

name: Bangladesh
summary_text: Bangladesh presents a high risk for trans visitors. Protests forced the ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024, and in the year after that change LGBTQ people faced increased vulnerability to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.  Hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground after the 2024 change. Trans people who had previously lived visibly were reported to be living in hiding.  The current national incident baseline is 260 documented human rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across Bangladesh in 2025. The conduct includes murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. The monitoring group JMBF, in its annual report published in April 2026, describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022.  Lethal violence against visible trans people continues. Prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district and widely known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025. Five unidentified individuals were accused.  Section 377 of the Penal Code on unnatural offences provides that whoever voluntarily has carnal intercourse against the order of nature with any man, woman or animal shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Penetration is sufficient to constitute the offence. Its ambit extends to any sexual union involving penile insertion, including consensual heterosexual fellatio and anal penetration. Parliament refused to overturn Section 377 in 2009 and 2013. Formal laws imposed in 1860 through the Indian Penal Code effective in 1862 were carried into the Pakistan Penal Code after the 1947 partition and retained in the legal code since 1971 independence.  It remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within Section 377. A foreign government country policy note of September 2023, updated in April 2026, records that ambiguity, noting that one international review read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to all genders.  The law is rarely enforced through prosecution but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ, including extortion and bullying of LGBTI individuals and those considered effeminate. Police have also used a suspicious behavior provision of the police code and have limited registration of LGBTI organizations.  Hijras have been legally recognised as a separate third gender alongside males and females since a cabinet meeting on 11 November 2013. Voter lists offer third gender options, and hijra candidates have run for government positions. In April 2019 hijra was introduced as a third gender option on voting forms for the first time to allow voting under proper gender identity. There are no policies outlining measures individuals must undergo to legally change gender on official documents, no clarity about who may qualify as a hijra, and no protections from discrimination for hijra. Other transgender communities beyond hijras remain unrecognised and unprotected from discrimination.  Extortion driven police violence affects visibly trans people. After hijras refused police extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala. On 17 September police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from expatriate carrying vehicles in Narayanganj, a traditional livelihood.  Policing reaches transit hubs. In April 2024 five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, as documented by JMBF.  Asylum grade country material records Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues. Members have received threatening messages by telephone, text and social media, with some harassed by police.  Bangladeshi law does not recognise same sex relationships, civil unions or domestic partnership, and does not provide any adoption route for same sex couples. Same sex couples have been detained and can face imprisonment or fine. Labour law prohibits wage discrimination on the basis of sex or disability but does not prohibit other discrimination based on sex, disability, social status, caste, sexual orientation or similar factors. There are no legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation.

sources.title: Penal Code, Section 377 ("Unnatural offences")
sources.documents: Criminalization of same-sex sexual activity in Bangladesh; punishment of life imprisonment or up to 10 years plus fine; applies to anal/oral sex regardless of gender/orientation, including consensual heterosexual fellatio/anal penetration.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Cited as inherited from British Indian Penal Code 1860 (effective 1862), carried into Pakistan Penal Code after 1947 partition, retained after 1971 independence; Parliament refused to overturn in 2009 and 2013. Full text quoted in article.

Labour law prohibits wage discrimination on the basis of sex or disability but does not prohibit other discrimination based on sex, disability, social status, caste, sexual orientation or similar factors. There are no legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation.
